claim: In the authors' two-dimensional steady-sliding model of a rigid cylinder on an adhesive linear-standard-viscoelastic half-plane, the normal-pressure field, contact eccentricity, and slope-mediated dissipation depend jointly and non-monotonically on normalized speed, adhesive interaction scale, normal load, and relaxed-to-instantaneous modulus ratio; intermediate speeds produce opening/closing-edge asymmetry that disappears in the low- and high-speed elastic limits. This is model-specific mechanistic evidence that spatial contact state and viscoelastic memory-related regime variables can matter when defining candidate history-state and tangential-margin representations, but it does not establish the decision value of such representations in SoftScan control, a shear-friction capacity, a pressure-centroid-to-wrench mapping, or deployment safety.
claim_locator: Abstract; model formulation and dimensionless groups; numerical results for pressure/contact eccentricity and friction versus speed, Maugis parameter, and load; discussion and conclusion
epistemic_status: Author-reported numerical-model result with qualitative experimental comparison; controller relevance beyond the stated adhesive viscoelastic line-contact model is an explicitly caveated inference.
problem_and_setting: A rigid radius-R cylinder slides steadily at speed v over a smooth adhesive viscoelastic half-plane in two-dimensional line contact under prescribed dimensionless normal load. Adhesion follows a rate-independent Lennard-Jones traction-separation law, and the substrate is a small-deformation linear standard solid with one relaxation time. The paper studies how relaxed Maugis-Tabor parameter, load, normalized speed, and modulus ratio affect normal-pressure asymmetry and the friction calculated from pressure acting on the deformed surface slope.
method_or_mechanism: The authors discretize the steady-moving viscoelastic half-plane Green-function solution with a boundary-element method, iteratively vary indentation to satisfy prescribed load, and compute friction as the integral of local normal pressure times deformed-surface slope. The mechanism is hysteretic bulk viscoelastic loss coupled to adhesive opening/closing-edge asymmetry; no interfacial tangential shear stress is present.
content_summary: The paper reduces the steady problem to four dimensionless controls: relaxed Maugis-Tabor parameter lambda, dimensionless load W, speed V, and modulus ratio k=E0/Einf. Pressure is symmetric in the relaxed and instantaneous elastic limits and becomes asymmetric near the viscoelastic transition. At intermediate speed, trailing/opening and leading/closing adhesive tractions differ, and changing lambda can alter both the magnitude and direction of contact eccentricity. The calculated friction is bell-shaped with log speed, can acquire a substantial adhesive contribution as lambda increases, and shows non-monotonic load and speed dependence at large lambda. The large-lambda adhesive contribution approaches the paper's stated JKR-like scaling at intermediate speed, while sharp pressure spikes create numerical discrepancies. Comparison with smooth-rubber experiments is qualitative, and the authors state that rubber-friction adhesion remains unclear and is often treated semi-empirically.
synthesis_role: Supports CHAIN-SPATIAL-SUFFICIENCY and CHAIN-HISTORY-SUFFICIENCY by showing, within a tightly specified adhesive viscoelastic line-contact model, that a scalar load alone does not determine the spatial pressure/contact state and that normalized speed relative to relaxation time changes the regime. It provides only indirect hypothesis-generating support for OBL-TANGENTIAL-MARGIN: the paper's slope-mediated normal-traction dissipation is not a tangential shear margin or wrench capacity. It does not test CHAIN-CLOSED-LOOP-ABSORPTION, the candidate empirical front/rear-patch equations, a proposed speed law, held-out continuous soft-contact shifts, or the independent scanning endpoint.
development_link: For P-SOFTSCAN-STATE-01 v1, motivates testing whether independent front/rear or local-geometry information and a short history/speed-relaxation state improve impedance selection beyond force/load-only feedback. Any front/rear patch statistic or speed-law term remains a candidate empirical representation requiring identification and held-out closed-loop comparison; this paper neither derives nor validates those SoftScan equations. A pressure-centroid or normal-pressure asymmetry signal must not be treated as a measured tangential-force, torsional, or bending safety margin without separate evidence.

evidence.finding: The solution and friction coefficient depend on relaxed Maugis-Tabor parameter, dimensionless load, normalized speed, and modulus ratio; adhesion becomes important at intermediate to large Maugis parameter, while agreement with experiment is qualitative.

evidence.locator: Model formulation: Lennard-Jones traction law, standard-linear-solid Green function, and friction integral
evidence.finding: The interface has nominally frictionless adhesive normal contact, and the reported friction is generated by normal pressure acting over the deformed surface slope rather than by interfacial shear traction.

evidence.locator: Numerical pressure results at low, intermediate, and high speed
evidence.finding: Pressure is symmetric in the low- and high-speed elastic limits and asymmetric at intermediate speed, with unequal trailing/opening and leading/closing tensile features and a leading compressive spike near the transition.

evidence.locator: Numerical lambda sweep at W=0.1 and k=0.1
evidence.finding: Increasing adhesive interaction strength changes traction sharpness and the magnitude and direction of contact eccentricity, demonstrating that spatial state is regime dependent within the model.

Friction is bell-shaped versus speed, gains an adhesive contribution as lambda increases, and can depend non-monotonically on load and speed; extremely sharp pressure spikes are associated with numerical discrepancies.

The authors report only qualitative agreement with smooth-rubber experiments, identify unresolved adhesive-friction physics, and exclude roughness, Schallamach bond-debonding, and Schallamach-wave mechanisms from the model.

Because equal load need not imply equal spatial pressure/contact state across speed and adhesion regimes, independent spatial and short-history variables are plausible candidate control features; their incremental decision value must still be established in SoftScan experiments and closed-loop comparisons.

boundary_conditions: Two-dimensional cylinder/half-plane line contact, not a finite three-dimensional probe footprint.
Steady unidirectional sliding only; no transient loading, acceleration, stopping, reversal, or loading-path experiment.
Smooth nominally frictionless adhesive interface; friction is slope-mediated normal-traction dissipation, not interfacial shear traction.
Small-deformation linear standard viscoelasticity with one relaxation time.
Rate-independent Lennard-Jones adhesion with a finite cohesive length scale.
No roughness, temperature-frequency shifting, multimode relaxation spectrum, Schallamach bond-debonding, or Schallamach waves.
Numerical discrepancies occur for extremely sharp pressure spikes.
Experimental comparison is qualitative and concerns smooth rubber/glass, not ultrasound tissue contact.
No robot, impedance controller, held-out shift protocol, force/wrench safety test, or imaging endpoint is studied.
assumptions: Rigid cylindrical indenter and viscoelastic half-plane geometry.
Linear standard-solid constitutive law characterized by relaxed and instantaneous moduli and one relaxation time.
Steady-moving Green-function representation and constant-pressure-element BEM discretization.
Prescribed normal load is enforced by iterative indentation adjustment.
Local adhesion is fully represented by the stated Lennard-Jones force-separation law.
Surface-slope integral of normal pressure is an adequate definition of friction for the modeled mechanism.
Dimensionless speed based on relaxation time and contact length adequately indexes the modeled rate regime.
Any SoftScan interpretation of front/rear patch, history, or speed features is an analogy to be tested, not an assumption established by this paper.

reported: Only qualitative agreement is obtained with the cited smooth-rubber experiments.
Rubber-friction adhesion remains unclear and is often modeled semi-empirically.
Extremely sharp pressure spikes cause numerical discrepancies.
The finite cohesive/crack length scale prevents a complete mapping to purely energetic JKR studies, and the authors do not expect entire low-speed curves to match.
The model lacks ingredients needed for rough-surface friction and excludes Schallamach-wave and chain bond-debonding mechanisms.
inferred: The results cannot validate the candidate SoftScan front/rear-patch contact equations or identify their minimally sufficient form.
The steady normalized-speed dependence cannot by itself validate a robot speed law under transients, reversals, tissue variability, or closed-loop impedance adaptation.

Pressure asymmetry or contact eccentricity cannot be equated with tangential force, torsional/bending wrench capacity, or a safety margin because the model contains no interfacial shear traction or measured wrench limit surface.

The paper cannot establish incremental controller decision value over simpler or model-agnostic feedback because it includes no controller comparison, held-out contact shifts, imaging endpoint, or deployment test.
Generalization from an adhesive viscoelastic cylinder/rubber setting to ultrasound probe-tissue contact is unsupported without separate empirical evidence.

conflicts_with: Conflicts with any claim that normal load alone uniquely determines contact state across viscoelastic speed and adhesion regimes within this model.
Conflicts with treating the paper's reported friction as a Coulomb coefficient, direct shear limit, or complete tangential wrench-capacity measurement.
Conflicts with presenting the paper as validation of SoftScan controller decision value, candidate front/rear equations, a deployment speed law, or ultrasound-tissue safety.
verification_status: verified against Controller-supplied admitted full text
